analysis.one_liner: Caps consumer loan interest rates, including fees, at the maximum each borrower's home state allows.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; after its June 2023 referral to the Senate Banking Committee, no action was taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill writes a single rule into federal law: for any consumer loan other than a home mortgage, the interest rate — including fees — cannot exceed the maximum allowed in the state where the borrower lives. That closes the current gap where banks and their lending partners can charge rates that a state has banned, such as triple-digit payday loan rates. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who borrow — especially payday, installment, auto-title, and credit card borrowers in states with low rate caps — would pay interest and fees no higher than their own state allows. The bill counts fees toward the cap, so lenders could not bury the cost in add-on charges. States that have voted to cap rates would have those caps enforced against lenders regardless of where the lender is chartered.

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps the annual percentage rate on every consumer credit transaction except home mortgages at the maximum rate allowed by the state where the borrower lives, with fees counted toward the cap.

The cap applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of law,' which targets the loophole where a lender chartered in a state with no rate cap — or a bank partnering with a high-rate lender — can export that high rate into states whose voters chose lower caps.

Because the cap travels with the borrower rather than the lender, it lets states that have already capped rates — for example, the roughly 18-20 states that cap payday-style lending at 36% or lower — actually enforce those caps against all lenders serving their residents.

analysis.who_pays: High-interest consumer lenders — payday, installment, and auto-title lenders, and the banks that partner with them to export rates above state caps — would lose revenue from loans they can no longer make at rates above a borrower's home-state limit. Some borrowers with poor credit would also bear a cost if lenders stop serving them rather than lend at capped rates.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection: binding rate caps can shrink credit supply. Lenders who cannot price for risk may stop serving borrowers with poor credit, pushing some people to borrow from unregulated or illegal sources instead of a payday loan.

The bill overrides lenders' existing contracts and pricing models nationwide, so its effects on credit availability in states that already allow high rates — where borrowers currently have access, at a price — are uncertain and were never studied in a hearing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in states that have already chosen to cap rates, the benefit is concrete: interest and fees on small loans would drop from rates that can run several hundred percent annually to the state maximum. The real cost falls on borrowers with poor credit, who might lose access to legal small-dollar credit if lenders exit rather than lend at capped rates — a tradeoff rate-cap debates turn on, and one a fair hearing would have weighed. The bill had no mechanism for that hearing; it never got one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Banking Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and was never brought up for a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 13, 2023, by Senator Whitehouse with four cosponsors, and was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Only five senators put their names on the bill — all Democrats plus independent Senator Sanders — and no Republican cosponsored it, leaving it without the broader support needed to reach the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-interest consumer lenders are better off, because the rate cap never advanced and the existing system — where bank-chartered lenders can charge rates a borrower's home state has banned — remains in place unchanged.

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to apply each state's maximum rate cap to consumer loans nationwide.

for.name: Jack Reed, Elizabeth Warren, Bernie Sanders, Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the Senate's progressive wing as its entire base of support.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee (Chair Sherrod Brown)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred, never holding a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all five sponsors were Democrats or the chamber's independent progressive, and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: Payday and auto-title lenders charge triple-digit annual rates that many states have banned; the bill would bar them from charging more than the borrower's home-state cap, with fees counted toward it.

industries.industry: National banks that partner with consumer lenders
industries.note: Some high-rate lenders issue loans through partner banks that can carry their home state's high rate into states with caps; the bill's 'notwithstanding any other provision of law' language would close that channel, cutting off a revenue stream those banks lease out.

industries.industry: Consumer credit and credit card issuers
industries.note: General-purpose credit card and consumer lenders operate across state lines under a single national rate structure; applying each borrower's home-state cap would force them to price differently by state and cap rates in states that limit them, though lenders could simply decline to serve those markets.
